---
title: "Setting Up the Methods Vault in VS Code"
---

## What is the Methods Vault?

The Methods Vault is your personal research workspace for this course. It is a VS Code workspace, cloned from a GitHub template, that keeps your journals, literature notes, project files, and reusable templates in one version-controlled folder. Everything is plain Markdown, so you own your data and can read it anywhere. With the **Foam** extension it also gains `[[wiki-links]]`, a backlinks panel, and a graph view, turning your notes into a connected research archive.

---

## Step 1: Install VS Code

If you have not already, follow the [Install VS Code](install-vscode.qmd) guide. You will also want R and Git installed, covered in [Install R](install-r.qmd) and [Getting Started with GitHub](github-setup.qmd).

---

## Step 2: Create your copy from the template

1. Go to the [v2v-methods-vault repository](https://github.com/AURA-Lab-SIUE/v2v-methods-vault).
2. Click **Use this template**, then **Create a new repository**.
3. Name it something like `mc451-methods-vault`. Private is fine.
4. Click **Create repository**.

You now have your own copy of the workspace on GitHub.

---

## Step 3: Clone it into VS Code

1. Copy your new repository's URL (the green **Code** button).
2. In VS Code, open the Command Palette: `Ctrl+Shift+P` (Windows) or `Cmd+Shift+P` (Mac).
3. Type **Git: Clone** and press Enter.
4. Paste your repository URL.
5. Choose a folder you will remember, for example `Documents/MC451/`.
6. When VS Code asks, click **Open** to open the cloned workspace.

---

## Step 4: Install the recommended extensions

When the workspace opens, VS Code shows a prompt in the bottom-right: **"This workspace has extension recommendations."** Click **Install All**. These are defined in `.vscode/extensions.json` so the whole class shares one environment:

| Extension | What it does |
|-----------|--------------|
| **Foam** | `[[wiki-links]]`, backlinks panel, and graph view across your notes |
| **Quarto** | Preview and render `.qmd` documents |
| **R** (REditorSupport) | Run R code and view data inside VS Code |
| **Markdown All in One** | Table of contents, shortcuts, and list editing for Markdown |

If you miss the prompt, open the Extensions view (`Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+X`), type `@recommended`, and install from there.

---

## Step 5: Read the start guide

Open `00_START_HERE.md` in the file explorer (left sidebar). It walks you through the folder structure, how to start a journal entry, and how Foam linking works.

The workspace is pre-organized:

- **00_Inbox** captures ideas quickly.
- **01_Journal** holds your weekly reflections (committed to GitHub).
- **02_Literature** holds reading notes and Zotero annotations.
- **03_Project** holds your active research work.
- **04_Resources** holds images, PDFs, and attachments.
- **_templates** holds reusable templates.

Follow this structure to stay organized.

---

## Step 6: Start a journal entry from the template

1. In the file explorer, open `_templates/journal-entry.md`.
2. Right-click it and choose **Copy**, then right-click the `01_Journal/` folder and choose **Paste**.
3. Rename the copy for the week, for example `week-02-curiosity-and-trust.md`.
4. Fill in the prompts. Use `[[` to link to a literature note or project file; Foam suggests existing notes as you type.

---

## Step 7: Connect your notes with Foam

Linking notes together is what turns a folder of files into a knowledge graph.

### Create a link

In any note, type `[[` and start typing a note name:

```markdown
# My research

I'm building on [[journal-entry]] to develop my reflection process,
and I reference my [[literature-review]] notes for sources.
```

Foam suggests existing notes. Select one, or type a new name to create a linked note.

### View backlinks and the graph

- The **Backlinks** panel (in the Foam sidebar) shows every note that links to the one you are viewing.
- Run **Foam: Show Graph** from the Command Palette to see your whole archive as a connected map.

---

## Step 8: Basic Markdown syntax

Notes use Markdown. The essentials:

| Syntax | Result |
|--------|--------|
| `# Heading 1` | Large heading |
| `## Heading 2` | Medium heading |
| `**Bold text**` | **Bold text** |
| `*Italic text*` | *Italic text* |
| `- List item` | Bullet list |
| `1. Numbered item` | Numbered list |
| `[Link text](https://example.com)` | Hyperlink |
| `[[Note name]]` | Link to another note (Foam) |
| `> Quote` | Block quote |
| `` `code` `` | Inline code |

VS Code shows a live preview with `Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+V`.

---

## Step 9: Commit and push your work

At the end of each week, save your work to GitHub. You can use VS Code's **Source Control** panel (the branch icon in the left bar): stage your changes, write a short message, and click **Commit**, then **Sync Changes**. Or use the terminal:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Week 2 journal and literature notes"
git push
```

This gives you a backup, a history of your work, and a way for Dr. Leith to see your entries. It also builds the version-control habit you will use in the final portfolio.

---

## Troubleshooting

### The extension prompt never appeared

Open the Extensions view (`Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+X`), type `@recommended`, and install the listed extensions.

### `[[wiki-links]]` are not autocompleting

Make sure Foam is installed and enabled, then reload the window (`Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P` then **Developer: Reload Window**).

### I cannot push to GitHub

Confirm you are signed in to GitHub in VS Code (the Accounts icon, bottom-left) and that you cloned **your** copy of the repository, not the original template.
